Notes: c. 170 BCE (date of Onias III's murder per Goldstein; some say 171). 2 Maccabees 4:33-38: the deposed high priest Onias III took refuge at the sanctuary of Daphne near Antioch and was murdered by Andronicus at Menelaus' instigation; 'the Jews in the city appealed to' Antiochus IV on his return from Cilicia (4:36; NRSVUE footnote: 'or in each city'). Earliest firm literary attestation of a Jewish community at Antioch able to petition the king. No count. [Review fix: Year Established changed from -300 to -170: first securely documented presence (2 Macc 4:33-38, c. 170 BCE); the claim of Jews from the foundation (c. 300 BCE, Josephus) is doubted by scholars]

c. 160 BCE (successors of Antiochus IV, after 164 BCE; approximate). Josephus, War 7.43-45: the Jews were especially numerous in Syria and above all in Antioch; Antiochus Epiphanes' successors restored to the Antiochene Jews the bronze votive offerings plundered from Jerusalem, which they laid up in their synagogue, and granted them civic rights equal to the Greeks; the community grew and attracted many Greek proselytes. Organized community with a (great) synagogue; ancient statement of large size, no number.

2nd c. BCE (midpoint -150). Encyclopaedia Judaica (A. Haim / D. Kushner, via Jewish Virtual Library): 'There must have been a considerable number of Jews in Antioch by the second century B.C.E.'; Jews' franchise engraved on bronze tablets in a public place; Josephus praises the beauty of its great synagogue; in the Roman period the Jewish population grew and was augmented by many proselytes. No figure given.

c. 145 BCE. 1 Maccabees 11:41-51: Jonathan sent 3,000 Judean soldiers to Antioch to aid Demetrius II against a revolt of the townspeople ('to the number of a hundred and twenty thousand'); the Jews killed 'about one hundred thousand', burned part of the city and returned to Jerusalem. These are a temporary Judean expeditionary force and clearly exaggerated ancient figures, not resident Jews - Population blank. Event likely aggravated local anti-Jewish feeling.

c. 9-6 BCE (governorship of C. Sentius Saturninus; midpoint). Josephus, Ant. 17.23-29: a Babylonian Jew (named Zamaris at 17.29) with 500 mounted archers and about 100 relatives crossed the Euphrates and 'abode at Antioch by Daphne of Syria', where Saturninus gave them a place called Valatha; Herod then moved them to Batanea. Temporary settlement near (not in) Antioch; group counts are not the city's Jewish population - Population blank.

Reign of Augustus (27 BCE-14 CE; midpoint c. -7). Modern scholarly estimate: D. K. Eng (Evangelical Review of Theology 42.3, 2018, p. 269): 'The 45,000 Jews living in Antioch during the reign of Augustus created pocket communities, most notably near the Daphne Gate', citing W. Meeks & R. Wilken, Jews and Christians in Antioch (1978) p. 8 (figure ultimately derived from C. H. Kraeling, JBL 51, 1932). Method not stated in this source (Kraeling's estimate rests on an assumed share of a total city population).

c. 33 CE (approximate). Acts 6:5: among the seven chosen in Jerusalem was 'Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch' - an individual convert to Judaism from Antioch (attests Jewish proselytism there). Individual-level presence; no count.

c. 35-40 CE (approximate). Acts 11:19-20: believers scattered after Stephen's death reached Antioch and 'spoke the word to no one except Jews', before others addressed the Hellenists/Greeks. Attests a Jewish community (synagogue audience) at Antioch; no count.

40 CE (Malalas: third year of Gaius/Caligula). Zondervan Encyclopedia of the Bible, 'Antioch (Syria)': 'In a.d. 40 an outbreak of rioting between the circus factions developed into a pogrom against the Jews'; the story that the Jerusalem high priest led a punitive expedition is called apocryphal. Anti-Jewish riot; community survived. No casualty or population figure.

c. 45 CE (context of Acts 11:19-30). C. S. Keener, Bible Backgrounds note: 'Perhaps 10% of Antioch was Jewish (though, like some other ancient population figures, this is merely an educated guess)'; many proselytes and God-fearers attended Antioch's synagogues; no total population given, so no absolute figure - Population blank.

c. 48-49 CE (Antioch incident; approximate). Galatians 2:11-13: Paul opposed Cephas (Peter) at Antioch, and 'the other Jews joined him' in withdrawing from table fellowship with gentiles. Attests Jewish (Jewish-Christian) residents at Antioch; no count.

1st c. CE (midpoint 50). D. K. Eng (ERT 2018): 'There is evidence of twenty to thirty synagogues in Antioch during the first century'; Greek- and Aramaic-speaking Jews; major synagogue in suburb of Daphne; most Jews labourers (citing Brooten 2000, Zetterholm 2003). Indicates a very large, internally diverse community. No count beyond the 45,000 estimate above.

1st c. CE (midpoint 50; context of Paul's time). Modern scholarly estimate: C. S. Keener, 'A Closer Look: Antioch' (2020): 'Josephus claims a very large Jewish population there; rough estimates generally range from 20,000 to 40,000.' Population = midpoint of range 20,000-40,000. Keener notes total-city estimates vary from 100,000-150,000 to 500,000-600,000 (not used).

66 CE, outbreak of the revolt. Josephus, War 2.479: amid massacres of Jews in Syrian cities, 'only the Antiochians, the Sidonians, and Apamians spared those that dwelt with them' and would neither kill nor imprison any Jews. Community intact; no count.

67 CE (when Vespasian had newly arrived in Syria). Josephus, War 7.46-53: Antiochus, a Jew and son of the archon (chief magistrate) of the Antiochene Jews, accused his father and others of plotting to burn the city; the accused were burned alive in the theatre, Jews were forced to sacrifice in the Greek manner (refusers killed) and to break the Sabbath. Anti-Jewish violence; deaths not counted; attests an organized community with its own archon.

c. 67-69 CE (Mucianus governor of Syria; 'the last war'). Josephus, Ant. 12.120: Jews of Antioch received money from the gymnasiarchs in lieu of foreign oil; when the Antiochenes tried to abolish this during the war, Mucianus preserved it; Ant. 12.121-124: later the people of Alexandria and Antioch asked Vespasian and Titus to revoke Jewish rights, which they refused. Community and privileges continued; no count.

c. 70 CE (under acting legate Cn. Pompeius Collega, before the new governor Caesennius Paetus took up office; approximate). Josephus, War 7.54-62: a fire destroyed the square market, archives and basilicas; Antiochus blamed the Jews and the mob attacked them; Collega's inquiry found the Jews innocent (debtors had set the fire), but the Jews remained in great fear. Event; no count.

Spring 71 CE (Titus at Antioch after the fall of Jerusalem). Josephus, War 7.100-111: the senate and people of Antioch begged Titus to expel the Jews and then to remove the bronze tablets recording their privileges; Titus refused both and 'permitted the Jews of Antioch to continue to enjoy the very same privileges'. Community remained; Population blank (not 0).
